```{r}
#| include: false
library(here); library(tidyverse); library(knitr)

d      <- read_csv(here("data/processed/wdi_clean.csv"))
fit    <- read_csv(here("results/tables/preston_fit.csv"))
gaps   <- read_csv(here("results/tables/income_group_gaps.csv"))
latest <- as.integer(readLines(here("results/tables/latest_year.txt")))

f1 <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)   # one-decimal formatter
f0 <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")

# Preston-curve fits (life expectancy on log income), 1990 and latest year
m0 <- lm(lifeexp ~ log(gdppc), data = filter(d, year == 1990))
m1 <- lm(lifeexp ~ log(gdppc), data = filter(d, year == latest))
pred  <- function(m, x) unname(predict(m, tibble(gdppc = x)))
shift <- function(x) pred(m1, x) - pred(m0, x)
dbl_0 <- fit$per_doubling[fit$year == 1990]
dbl_1 <- fit$per_doubling[fit$year == latest]
r2_0  <- summary(m0)$r.squared
r2_1  <- summary(m1)$r.squared
n_0   <- sum(d$year == 1990); n_1 <- sum(d$year == latest)

# Country changes (countries observed in both years)
common <- inner_join(filter(d, year == 1990), filter(d, year == latest),
                     by = "country", suffix = c("_0", "_1")) |>
  mutate(dle = lifeexp_1 - lifeexp_0)
n_common <- nrow(common)
mean_gain <- mean(common$dle)
share_up  <- mean(common$dle > 0)
cn <- function(x) common[common$country == x, ]

# Residuals in latest year
d1 <- filter(d, year == latest) |> mutate(resid = residuals(m1))
nig_res <- d1$resid[d1$country == "Nigeria"]
nig_rank <- rank(d1$resid)[d1$country == "Nigeria"]

# Income groups
grp <- d |> group_by(income, year) |>
  summarise(le = weighted.mean(lifeexp, pop), .groups = "drop")
g <- function(inc, y) grp$le[grp$income == inc & grp$year == y]
gap_0 <- gaps$gap_high_low[gaps$year == 1990]
gap_1 <- gaps$gap_high_low[gaps$year == latest]
gain  <- function(inc) g(inc, latest) - g(inc, 1990)
```

## Question and motivation

Richer countries tend to have healthier populations. But how tight is that link, does it flatten out
at high incomes, and have poor countries been catching up with rich ones? These questions matter for
policy. If life expectancy depends mainly on income, then economic growth is the main route to better
health. If instead the whole relationship shifts over time (through vaccines, sanitation, cheap
medicines), then health can improve even where growth is slow.

The cross-country relationship between income and life expectancy is called the **Preston curve**.
I use it to ask: *how has the link between income and life expectancy changed between 1990 and
`r latest`, and have poorer countries caught up?*

## Data

All data come from the World Bank's World Development Indicators (WDI) and are downloaded
programmatically with the R package `WDI` (`code/01_get_data.R`):

- **GDP per capita, PPP, constant 2021 international dollars.** Dividing by population removes the
  effect of country size; PPP adjusts for differences in price levels across countries; using
  *constant* dollars removes inflation so that 1990 and `r latest` are comparable.
- **Life expectancy at birth** (years).
- **Population**, used for bubble sizes and population-weighted averages.

I drop World Bank aggregates (e.g., "World," regional groupings) and keep country-years with all three
variables. The sample has `r n_0` countries in 1990 and `r n_1` in `r latest`; the `r n_common` countries
present in both years are used when I follow countries over time. GDP is plotted on a **log scale**
because an extra $1,000 matters far more to a country with $2,000 per person than one with $60,000.
Accordingly, I model life expectancy as a linear function of log income.

## Figure 1: The cross-section in `r latest`

```{r}
#| echo: false
include_graphics(here("results/figures/fig1_preston_latest.png"))
```

Life expectancy rises steeply with income at the low end and more gently at the top. Countries below
about $5,000 per person range from the mid-50s to the low 70s in life expectancy, while countries
above $50,000 are mostly in the high 70s and 80s. In a regression of life expectancy on log GDP per capita,
**doubling income is associated with about `r f1(dbl_1)` additional years of life**, and income alone
accounts for roughly `r round(100 * r2_1)`% of the cross-country variation in life expectancy ($R^2$ = `r round(r2_1, 2)`).

That leaves a lot unexplained. Nigeria, for example, lies about `r f0(abs(nig_res))` years below the
fitted line, the largest negative gap in the sample, while its income per person (about
$`r f0(d1$gdppc[d1$country == "Nigeria"])`) is similar to India's, where life expectancy is
`r f1(d1$lifeexp[d1$country == "India"])` years versus Nigeria's
`r f1(d1$lifeexp[d1$country == "Nigeria"])`. The United States sits below the line too: it is among the
richest countries, but its life expectancy (`r f1(d1$lifeexp[d1$country == "United States"])`) is lower than that of
many poorer countries. So income matters, but it is not destiny. This is a correlation, not a causal effect, and health also
affects income.

## Figure 2: The curve has shifted up

```{r}
#| echo: false
include_graphics(here("results/figures/fig2_curve_shift.png"))
```

Figure 2 plots 1990 (orange) and `r latest` (green) together. Two things stand out.

**1. The whole curve moved up.** At the same income, countries live longer today. A country with
$1,000 per person would have been predicted to have a life expectancy of `r f1(pred(m0, 1000))` years
in 1990 but `r f1(pred(m1, 1000))` years in `r latest`, a shift of `r f1(shift(1000))` years. At $5,000 the shift is
`r f1(shift(5000))` years and at $50,000 it is `r f1(shift(50000))` years. The upward shift is **largest for the poorest
countries**, which suggests that improvements in health technology and public health have benefited low-income countries the most.
Among the `r n_common` countries observed in both years, the average gain in life expectancy was
`r f1(mean_gain)` years, and `r round(100 * share_up)`% of countries improved.

**2. The curve became flatter and tighter.** The slope fell from `r f1(dbl_0)` years per doubling of income in 1990
to `r f1(dbl_1)` years in `r latest`, and the $R^2$ rose from `r round(r2_0, 2)` to `r round(r2_1, 2)`.
The same income gap now translates into a smaller life-expectancy gap.

The arrows show that individual countries moved both right (growth) and up (health), but not equally.
India went from `r f1(cn("India")$lifeexp_0)` to `r f1(cn("India")$lifeexp_1)` years as income per person rose from
$`r f0(cn("India")$gdppc_0)` to $`r f0(cn("India")$gdppc_1)`. China rose from `r f1(cn("China")$lifeexp_0)` to
`r f1(cn("China")$lifeexp_1)` years while income grew more than ten-fold. Korea went from
`r f1(cn("Korea, Rep.")$lifeexp_0)` to `r f1(cn("Korea, Rep.")$lifeexp_1)`. In contrast, the United States gained only
`r f1(cn("United States")$dle)` years even though income rose by about
`r round(100 * (cn("United States")$gdppc_1 / cn("United States")$gdppc_0 - 1))`%, and Nigeria's life expectancy
(`r f1(cn("Nigeria")$lifeexp_0)` to `r f1(cn("Nigeria")$lifeexp_1)`) remains the lowest among the countries I highlight even though its income increased.
Within this period, growth and health gains are clearly linked but not mechanically.

## Figure 3: Have income groups converged?

```{r}
#| echo: false
include_graphics(here("results/figures/fig3_income_groups.png"))
```

Population-weighted life expectancy rose in all four income groups, and the poorer groups gained the most:
`r f1(gain("Low income"))` years in low-income countries, `r f1(gain("Lower middle income"))` in lower-middle-income,
`r f1(gain("Upper middle income"))` in upper-middle-income, and `r f1(gain("High income"))` in high-income countries.
As a result, the gap between high- and low-income countries **shrank from `r f1(gap_0)` years in 1990 to
`r f1(gap_1)` years in `r latest`**. The gaps are still large, however: people in low-income countries live
about `r f1(gap_1)` fewer years than those in high-income countries.

The figure also shows the effect of COVID-19. Between 2019 and 2021, life expectancy fell by
`r f1(g("Lower middle income", 2019) - g("Lower middle income", 2021))` years in lower-middle-income countries,
`r f1(g("High income", 2019) - g("High income", 2021))` years in high-income countries and
`r f1(g("Upper middle income", 2019) - g("Upper middle income", 2021))` years in upper-middle-income countries,
and low-income countries saw a small decline. By `r latest`, all four groups were at or above their 2019 levels, so the pandemic interrupted but did not reverse the long-run convergence.

## Takeaway

Income and life expectancy are strongly and non-linearly related: each doubling of income is associated with
about `r f1(dbl_1)` more years of life in `r latest`, and gains are largest at low incomes. But income is not the whole
story. Since 1990, the entire curve has shifted upward (by about `r f1(shift(1000))` years for the poorest
countries versus `r f1(shift(50000))` years for the richest), the relationship between income and life expectancy has become flatter, and
the high-to-low-income gap fell by about `r f1(gap_0 - gap_1)` years. Poor countries have therefore caught up
substantially in health, even though a large gap remains.

For policy, this suggests that low-cost health improvements (vaccines, sanitation, basic
care) can raise life expectancy even where income growth is slow, while economic growth still matters, particularly
at low income levels. Outliers like Nigeria show that income alone does not determine health outcomes.

**Limitations.** The analysis is descriptive, not causal. Income groups use the World Bank's *current*
classification, so a country that became richer is counted in the high-income group for all years. The sample of countries differs slightly
between 1990 and `r latest` (`r n_0` vs. `r n_1`). Finally, national averages hide
differences within countries.
